ch47.title: Gethsemane
ch47.b001: Thursday, Ten O’Clock at Night, Across the Kidron
ch47.b002: It was about ten o’clock on Thursday night when Jesus led the eleven out of the home of Elijah and Mary Mark. John Mark, who had snatched a few hours of sleep while the Master was with his apostles in the upper room, heard them coming down the stairs. He jumped up, threw a linen coat about himself, and followed them through the sleeping city, over the brook Kidron, and on to their camp beside Gethsemane Park. Ever since that day in the hills he had made it his business to keep a watchful eye on Jesus, and through this night and the following day he stayed so close that he witnessed everything and overheard much of what the Master said.
ch47.b003: On the way back the apostles began to wonder about Judas’s long absence. For the first time they suspected that all was not well with him. When they reached the camp and found that he was not there waiting for them, they all besieged Andrew to know what had become of him. Their chief said only, “⟦Q 182:0.2⟧I do not know where Judas is, but I fear he has deserted us.⟦/Q⟧”
ch47.b005: A few moments later Jesus said: “⟦Q 182:1.1⟧My friends and brethren, my time with you is now very short, and I desire that we draw apart by ourselves while we pray to our Father in heaven for strength to sustain us in this hour and henceforth in all the work we must do in his name.⟦/Q⟧” He led them a short way up Olivet, and in full view of Jerusalem he bade them kneel in a circle about him on a large flat rock, as they had done on the day of their ordination. Then, standing in their midst in the mellow moonlight, he lifted his eyes toward heaven and prayed:

ch47.b006.en: “Father, my hour has come; now glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you. … You gave me twelve men, and I have kept them all save one, the son of revenge, who would not have further fellowship with us. … The world may hate them, even as it has hated me, but I do not ask that you take them out of the world, only that you keep them from the evil in the world. Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. … I want them all to be one, even as you and I are one.”

ch47.b007: The eleven stayed on their knees for several minutes after he had finished. Then they rose and went back to the camp in silence. The words “the son of revenge” had opened their eyes: Judas had forsaken them. Jesus prayed for unity among his followers, but he did not desire uniformity. In that prayer he said that he had manifested the Father’s name to the world. To Moses the Father could reveal no more than “I AM.” But through his life in the flesh Jesus could say: I am the bread of life. I am the light of the world. I am the good shepherd. I am the way, the truth, and the life.
ch47.b009: While the eleven argued heatedly about their faithless brother, David Zebedee and John Mark drew Jesus aside and told him that they had been watching Judas for several days and knew he meant to betray him. Jesus listened, then said only: “⟦Q 182:2.1⟧My friends, nothing can happen to the Son of Man unless the Father in heaven so wills. Let not your hearts be troubled; all things will work together for the glory of God and the salvation of men.⟦/Q⟧”
ch47.b010: His cheerfulness was waning; as the hour passed he grew more and more serious, even sorrowful. He sent the apostles to their tents, asking Peter, James, and John to stay with him a little while. Before they went to bed, Simon Zelotes led the others to his tent, where the swords were stored, and gave each of them a weapon. Only Nathaniel refused. “⟦Q 182:2.3⟧I will pray, but I will not wield the sword.⟦/Q⟧” Hearing this, Andrew handed his sword back to Simon. So nine of them were armed when they went to sleep.
ch47.b011: Then Jesus asked David for his swiftest and most trustworthy messenger, and David brought him Jacob, who had once run the overnight route between Jerusalem and Bethsaida. Jesus gave him a message for Abner at Philadelphia: the hour had come when the Master would be delivered into the hands of his enemies and put to death, but he would rise from the dead and appear to Abner shortly, before he went to the Father. When Jacob had repeated it to the Master’s satisfaction, Jesus sent him off. “⟦Q 182:2.5⟧Fear not what any man may do to you, Jacob, for this night an unseen messenger will run by your side.⟦/Q⟧” He spoke a word of comfort to the leader of the Greeks encamped with them, and to Andrew he said: “⟦Q 182:2.8⟧Andrew, do what you can to keep your brethren together until I come again to you after I have drunk this cup.⟦/Q⟧”
ch47.b012: The apostles expected nothing to happen that night; they thought the chief priests would try to seize the Master early in the morning. Only David and John Mark knew that Judas was coming with the guards that very night. David took up watch on the upper trail toward the Bethany road, and as he went he told Jesus that he had sent for his family, who were now at Jericho and would arrive early the next morning. Jesus looked down at him and said only, “Let it be so, David.” John Mark was to watch the road by the Kidron. But when he saw Jesus withdraw into a nearby ravine with Peter, James, and John, his devotion and curiosity overcame him. He left his post, followed them, and hid in the bushes.
ch47.b013: Could You Not Watch One Hour?
ch47.b014: When all was quiet, Jesus took the three a short way up the ravine where he had often gone to pray. They had never seen him so heavy-laden and sorrowful. He bade them sit down and watch while he went about a stone’s throw away, and there he fell on his face and prayed: “⟦Q 182:3.1⟧My Father, I came into this world to do your will, and so have I. I know that the hour has come to lay down this life in the flesh, and I do not shrink therefrom, but I would know that it is your will that I drink this cup.⟦/Q⟧”
ch47.b015: After a few moments he came back and found them sound asleep. “⟦Q 182:3.2⟧What! can you not watch with me even for one hour? Cannot you see that my soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death, and that I crave your companionship?⟦/Q⟧” Again he went apart and fell on the ground: “⟦Q 182:3.2⟧Father, I know it is possible to avoid this cup—all things are possible with you—but I have come to do your will, and while this is a bitter cup, I would drink it if it is your will.⟦/Q⟧” Then a mighty angel came down beside him, touched him, and strengthened him. Among other things the angel told him that the Father desired his Son to finish his earth bestowal by passing through the experience of death, just as all mortal creatures must.
ch47.b016: Once more he found the three asleep. Once more he withdrew and prayed: “⟦Q 182:3.4⟧Father, you see my sleeping apostles; have mercy upon them. The spirit is indeed willing, but the flesh is weak. And now, O Father, if this cup may not pass, then would I drink it. Not my will, but yours, be done.⟦/Q⟧”
ch47.b017: No mortal can presume to understand what the incarnate Son of God thought and felt in that hour, but we know that he suffered untold sorrow, for the sweat rolled off his face in great drops. He was weary from long labor and anxious for the safety of his apostles. He knew how weak and ignorant they were, and he dreaded to leave them. He was cut off from his family in the flesh; one of his chosen associates was betraying him; his father Joseph’s people had rejected him. In this great sorrow his mind went back to his childhood in Nazareth, to Capernaum and Mount Hermon, to the sunrise and sunset on the shimmering Sea of Galilee, and with these memories he soothed his human heart. He was fully determined to use none of his sovereign power as the head of a universe to save himself. Above the garden hovered the assembled hosts of a vast creation, under orders not to interfere unless Jesus himself commanded it.
ch47.b018: When he returned the third time, they were still asleep. He looked at them with pity and said tenderly, “⟦Q 182:3.4⟧Sleep on now and take your rest; the time of decision is past.⟦/Q⟧” Then he reached down to shake them awake. “⟦Q 182:3.4⟧Arise, let us be going back to the camp, for, behold, he who betrays me is at hand, and the hour has come when my flock shall be scattered.⟦/Q⟧” Before Judas and the soldiers arrived, the Master had fully regained his customary poise. The spirit had triumphed over the flesh.
ch47.b020: Judas, on leaving the supper, had gone straight to his cousin, and the two of them to the captain of the temple guards. But when they reached the Mark home, Jesus and the eleven had left fully fifteen minutes before. Judas grew afraid. He knew that more than sixty devoted disciples were camped at Gethsemane and that Simon Zelotes kept a store of arms, and he was a coward at heart. He asked for forty armed soldiers. The Jewish rulers went to the Roman commander at the fortress of Antonia, who refused and sent them to his superior, and more than an hour passed before they finally reached Pilate himself. His wife had asked him not to grant the request, but since the presiding officer of the Sanhedrin had come in person, he agreed. About half past eleven Judas set out from the temple with more than sixty men: temple guards, Roman soldiers, and curious servants of the chief priests.
ch47.b021: At the camp two excited messengers had arrived looking for David, and the three apostles were now wide awake. The Greeks had posted a sentinel, and they poured out of their tents fully dressed and armed. Peter wanted to wake the other eight, but Jesus definitely forbade it. When his followers would not go back to their tents, he left them and walked down alone to the olive press near the entrance to Gethsemane Park. He wanted to be taken without his apostles being drawn into the struggle and arrested with him. He sat down on the olive press to wait, seen only by John Mark, hidden in a small shed nearby, and by an innumerable host of celestial observers.
ch47.b023: Torches and lanterns swung around the brow of the hill. Judas strode out well ahead of the band; he hoped to seem to have hurried ahead to warn his brethren. From the other side Peter, James, and John, with some thirty of their fellow campers, rushed down toward the olive press where the Master sat alone in the moonlight. There the two groups stood, with Jesus between them.
ch47.b024: Before Judas could reach him, Jesus made one last effort to save him from the act. He stepped aside and asked the Roman captain, “Whom do you seek?” The captain answered, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus stepped up directly in front of him and, in calm majesty, said, “I am he.” Those in the front ranks fell suddenly backward. There was now no need for Judas at all. But the traitor had to account for his presence and make a show of keeping his bargain, so he stepped up, placed a kiss upon the Master’s brow, and said, “Hail, Master and Teacher.” Jesus said, “⟦Q 183:3.5⟧Friend, is it not enough to do this! Would you even betray the Son of Man with a kiss?⟦/Q⟧”
ch47.b025: For a moment no one moved. Then Jesus, freeing himself from the traitor’s embrace, again asked, “Whom do you seek?” Again the captain said, “Jesus of Nazareth.” “⟦Q 183:3.6⟧I have told you that I am he. If, therefore, you seek me, let these others go their way. I am ready to go with you.⟦/Q⟧” The Roman captain was willing to let the apostles go in peace. But Malchus, the Syrian bodyguard of the high priest, stepped up to bind Jesus’ hands behind his back. Peter drew his sword, and the others rushed forward with him. Jesus raised a forbidding hand. “⟦Q 183:3.7⟧Peter, put up your sword. They who take the sword shall perish by the sword. Do you not understand that it is the Father’s will that I drink this cup? And do you not further know that I could even now command more than twelve legions of angels and their associates, who would deliver me from the hands of these few men?⟦/Q⟧”
ch47.b026: Alarmed, the captain of the guards had Jesus seized and bound with heavy cords. “⟦Q 183:3.8⟧Why do you come out against me with swords and with staves as if to seize a robber? I was daily with you in the temple, publicly teaching the people, and you made no effort to take me.⟦/Q⟧” When the captain ordered his followers seized as well, they fled into the ravine. As the guards started back, John Mark slipped out of the shed, and a soldier caught hold of his linen coat. The young man tore free of the garment and escaped naked, leaving the soldier holding the empty coat.
ch47.b028: John Mark ran to David on the upper trail, and together they woke the eight sleeping apostles. All of them gathered by the olive press. Simon Zelotes climbed onto the stone wall and pleaded with them to hurry after the mob and rescue the Master. But Nathaniel reminded them of Jesus’ teaching on nonresistance and of his charge that very night to preserve their lives for the work ahead, and James told how Jesus had bidden Peter sheathe his sword. At last Thomas pointed out that they could do nothing, since the Master would neither let his friends defend him nor use his divine powers against his enemies. He persuaded them to scatter, every man for himself, while David kept the camp as a messenger headquarters. By half past two in the morning the camp was deserted. Five apostles hid in Bethpage and Bethany; four hid in the city. Surely, the shepherd was smitten and the sheep were scattered.
ch47.b029: Peter and John, who had hidden among the olive trees, followed the mob back toward the city, John close behind, Peter afar off. John Mark took a cloak from their tent, cut around through the olive orchards, and was hiding near the gate of the high priest’s palace before the procession arrived.
ch47.b030: Before leaving the garden, the two captains had disputed where to take the prisoner. The captain of the temple guards wanted him brought to Caiaphas; the Roman captain ordered him taken to Annas, the former high priest, and the Roman’s orders were obeyed. Judas marched near the captains, but neither would so much as speak to him. When John Zebedee hurried up beside Jesus, the Jewish captain ordered him bound, but the Roman captain stopped it. “⟦Q 183:5.3⟧This man is neither a traitor nor a coward. … The Roman law allows that any prisoner may have at least one friend to stand with him before the judgment bar, and this man shall not be prevented from standing by the side of his Master, the prisoner.⟦/Q⟧” Hearing this, Judas was so ashamed that he dropped back behind the marchers and came up to the palace of Annas alone.
ch47.b031: So, under Roman protection, John was able to stay near Jesus right up to his death on the cross. And all the way to the palace of Annas, Jesus opened not his mouth. From the time of his arrest to the time of his appearance before Annas, the Son of Man spoke no word.
ch48.title: The Trials
ch48.b001: Before Dawn on Friday, the Palace of Annas
ch48.b002: Representatives of Annas had secretly instructed the Roman captain to bring Jesus straight to the palace of Annas on Mount Olivet, not far from the garden where he had been arrested. The former high priest, enriched by the temple revenues and father-in-law of Caiaphas, the acting high priest, was the most powerful single individual in all Jewry. He did not trust so important a matter wholly to his brusque and aggressive son-in-law. Besides, the Sanhedrin could not lawfully be convened before the morning sacrifice in the temple, which was offered about three o’clock. Meanwhile some thirty members of the Sanhedrin, all of them strongly and openly opposed to Jesus, had gathered by midnight at the palace of Caiaphas to wait.
ch48.b003: John Zebedee moved freely about the palace of Annas. The Roman captain had given his word for him, and besides, John and his brother James were well known to the older servants, for the former high priest was a distant relative of their mother, Salome.
ch48.b004: Annas entered his spacious audience chamber, seated himself in a large chair, and ordered the prisoner brought before him. When Jesus was young, Annas had taken a great interest in him. But Jesus had lately driven the money-changers from the temple, and that had threatened his revenues far more than any teaching. He had thought he might persuade Jesus to leave Palestine rather than die. When he stood before the stalwart and determined Galilean, he knew at once that it would be useless. Jesus was even more majestic and well poised than Annas remembered him.
ch48.b005: After surveying him in silence, Annas said: “⟦Q 184:1.4⟧You realize that something must be done about your teaching since you are disturbing the peace and order of our country.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus looked full into his eyes but made no reply. “⟦Q 184:1.4⟧What are the names of your disciples, besides Simon Zelotes, the agitator?⟦/Q⟧” Again Jesus did not answer. Annas, much disturbed, asked whether he had no regard for the power he held over the coming trial. Then Jesus said: “⟦Q 184:1.5⟧Annas, you know that you could have no power over me unless it were permitted by my Father. Some would destroy the Son of Man because they are ignorant; they know no better, but you, friend, know what you are doing. How can you, therefore, reject the light of God?⟦/Q⟧”
ch48.b006: The kindness of his manner almost bewildered Annas, but he pressed on and asked what Jesus was trying to teach. Jesus answered that he had spoken openly to the world, in the synagogues and in the temple; why not ask those who had heard him? At that the chief steward of the palace struck him in the face with his hand. “⟦Q 184:1.6⟧How dare you answer the high priest with such words?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said, “⟦Q 184:1.6⟧My friend, if I have spoken evil, bear witness against the evil; but if I have spoken the truth, why, then, should you smite me?⟦/Q⟧” Annas was too proud to rebuke his steward. In his confusion he went into another room and left Jesus alone with the attendants and guards for almost an hour. When he returned, he asked, “⟦Q 184:1.8⟧I have been told that you have claimed to be the Messiah; is that true?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus looked at him and only replied, “So you have said.” Messengers had come from Caiaphas, and as day was nearing, Annas sent Jesus to him, bound, in the custody of the temple guards.
ch48.b008: As the band had approached the palace of Annas, Judas, lagging behind, came up to the gate, saw Jesus and John, and went on to the house of Caiaphas. Soon after, Simon Peter arrived. He had thrown away his sword shortly before reaching the gate. John saw him standing there and asked the portress to let him in, and she gladly did so. The night was chilly, and Peter went over to the charcoal fire in the courtyard to warm himself among the servants of the high priest. He felt very much out of place there, and indeed he was. The Master had told John to stay near, but not Peter. His mind was in a whirl; he could scarcely believe that Jesus had been arrested.
ch48.b009: The portress came over to him and asked mischievously, “⟦Q 184:2.4⟧Are you not also one of this man’s disciples?⟦/Q⟧” Startled, with only one thought in his mind—to escape with his life—Peter answered, “I am not.” Soon another servant asked whether he had not seen him in the garden. Peter vehemently denied it: “⟦Q 184:2.5⟧I know not this man, neither am I one of his followers.⟦/Q⟧” Then the portress drew him aside and said that her sister had seen him in the temple with Jesus. With much cursing and swearing Peter denied it again: “⟦Q 184:2.6⟧I am not this man’s follower; I do not even know him; I never heard of him before.⟦/Q⟧” Later, when he came back to the fire to get warm, a man standing there told him that his speech betrayed him as a Galilean, and again he denied all connection with his Master.
ch48.b010: To get away from his accusers, he went off and stayed by himself on the porch. For more than an hour he walked up and down, thinking only how cleverly he had eluded the servants. Then the gate-keeper and her sister came upon him and teasingly charged him again, and once more he denied it. Just then the cock crowed, and Peter remembered the words his Master had spoken to him earlier that night. As he stood there, heavy of heart and crushed with guilt, the palace doors opened and the guards led Jesus past on the way to Caiaphas. By the light of the torches Jesus saw the despair on Peter’s face, and he turned and looked upon him. Peter never forgot that look as long as he lived. It was a glance of mingled pity and love such as mortal man had never seen on the Master’s face.
ch48.b011: Peter followed for a short distance, but he could go no farther. He sat down by the side of the road and wept bitterly. Then he turned back toward the camp, hoping to find Andrew. All this took place in the courtyard of the palace of Annas on Mount Olivet; Peter never went to the palace of Caiaphas. That a cock’s crowing woke him to what he had done shows that it happened outside Jerusalem, since it was against the law to keep poultry within the city. Peter never fully believed that he could be forgiven until he met his Master after the resurrection and saw that he was received just as before.
ch48.b013: At about half past three on Friday morning Caiaphas called the court to order in his palace. It was not a regular meeting of the Sanhedrin, nor was it held in the chamber of hewn stone in the temple; it was a special court of some thirty Sanhedrists, and Caiaphas sat more as prosecutor than as judge. Jesus was brought in wearing his usual garments, his hands bound behind his back, and the whole court was startled by his majestic appearance. They had never seen such composure in a man on trial for his life. John Zebedee stood with him throughout.
ch48.b014: Jewish law required that two witnesses agree on any point before a charge could be laid, and it forbade the testimony of a traitor, so Judas could not be used. More than a score of false witnesses came forward, but their testimony was so contradictory that the Sanhedrists themselves were ashamed. Jesus looked down benignly upon them and never said a word. Only two came near agreement, testifying that he had said he would “⟦Q 184:3.7⟧destroy this temple made with hands and in three days make another temple without hands.⟦/Q⟧” That was not exactly what Jesus had said, and he had pointed to his own body when he spoke. The high priest shouted at him, “⟦Q 184:3.8⟧Do you not answer any of these charges?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus opened not his mouth.
ch48.b015: At last Caiaphas could no longer endure that perfect composure and unbroken silence. He rushed over to Jesus and, shaking his finger in the Master’s face, said: “⟦Q 184:3.14⟧I adjure you, in the name of the living God, that you tell us whether you are the Deliverer, the Son of God.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered: “⟦Q 184:3.14⟧I am. Soon I go to the Father, and presently shall the Son of Man be clothed with power and once more reign over the hosts of heaven.⟦/Q⟧” Of all the questions put to him that night, this was the only one he answered plainly, for it concerned his bestowal mission.
ch48.b016: The high priest tore his outer garments. “⟦Q 184:3.15⟧What further need have we of witnesses? Behold, now have you all heard this man’s blasphemy. What do you now think should be done with this lawbreaker and blasphemer?⟦/Q⟧” They all answered in unison, “⟦Q 184:3.15⟧He is worthy of death; let him be crucified.⟦/Q⟧” Caiaphas stepped forward and struck Jesus in the face, and as the members of the court filed out of the room, they spat in his face and mockingly slapped him with the palms of their hands. Even Annas was shocked. So, in disorder, the first session ended at half past four.
ch48.b018: Jewish law required a second session on the day after the first, the time between to be spent in fasting and mourning. These men waited only one hour. During that hour Jesus was left in the audience chamber with the temple guards and the high priest’s servants, who mocked him, spat on him, and struck him in the face with a rod, saying, “⟦Q 184:4.1⟧Prophesy to us, you the Deliverer, who it was that struck you.⟦/Q⟧” When the abuse began, Jesus nodded to John to withdraw, knowing that John’s indignation would break out and probably cost him his life. John waited in lonely terror in the next room.
ch48.b019: Throughout that awful hour Jesus uttered no word. To his gentle and sensitive soul, there was no more bitter portion of his cup of humiliation. A shudder of indignation swept out over a vast universe as the celestial intelligences watched their beloved Sovereign submit to his ignorant and misguided creatures. He was undefending, but not defenseless; uncontending, but not vanquished. Having lived a life revealing God to man, he was now making a new and unprecedented revelation of man to God.
ch48.b020: At half past five the court reassembled while Jesus waited in the adjoining room with John and the guards. Annas reminded them that a charge of blasphemy would carry no weight with Pilate. In half an hour, without hearing any witnesses and with the prisoner absent, they drew up three charges: that he perverted the nation and incited the people to rebellion; that he taught the people to refuse tribute to Caesar; and that by claiming to be a king he incited treason against the emperor. Three Pharisees then took their leave; they wanted Jesus destroyed, but they would not frame charges without witnesses and in his absence. Judas was present, but he gave no testimony. At six o’clock Jesus was led out of the house of Caiaphas.
ch48.b021: Six in the Morning, the Praetorium
ch48.b022: Shortly after six o’clock on Friday morning, April 7, A.D. 30, Jesus was brought bound before Pontius Pilate, the Roman procurator of Judea, followed by about fifty of his accusers, among them Caiaphas and Judas Iscariot, and accompanied by the Apostle John. The public trial was held on the steps in front of the praetorium, beside the fortress of Antonia, because the Jews would not enter a gentile building where leaven might be used on the day of preparation for the Passover. They were not troubled in conscience as they plotted a judicial murder, yet they were scrupulous about ceremonial cleanness.
ch48.b023: Pilate was a fairly good administrator but a moral coward. He did not love the Jews and never understood them. Early in his rule he had blundered again and again: bringing Caesar’s images on his soldiers’ banners into Jerusalem and then removing them when the Jews offered to die rather than allow it, hanging the emperor’s shields on Herod’s palace until Rome ordered them taken down, taking money from the temple treasury for an aqueduct. The Jews had learned that when they threatened an uprising or an appeal to the emperor, he would give way. Years later, recalled to Rome after a needless slaughter of Samaritans, he never fully recovered from the regretful memory of having consented to the death of Jesus, and he at last took his own life.
ch48.b024: Pilate came out and asked, “⟦Q 185:2.1⟧What accusation do you bring against this fellow?⟦/Q⟧” The spokesman answered only, “⟦Q 185:2.1⟧If this man were not an evildoer, we should not have delivered him up to you.⟦/Q⟧” Then let them judge him by their own law, said Pilate, and he took some pleasure in making them confess publicly that it was not lawful for them to put any man to death. But he would not sentence a man without a trial, and he demanded the charges in writing. The clerk of the court handed them over, and Pilate had them repeated in Jesus’ hearing. Jesus had never been heard on any of them, yet he made no reply, even when Pilate bade him answer. Astonished at the unfairness of it all and impressed by the prisoner’s silent and masterly bearing, Pilate decided to examine him privately.
ch48.b026: He took Jesus and John into a private chamber, asked the prisoner to sit down, and sat beside him. He began by saying he did not believe the first charge. Then he asked whether Jesus had ever taught that tribute should be refused to Caesar. Jesus pointed to John: “⟦Q 185:3.1⟧Ask him or any other man who has heard my teaching.⟦/Q⟧” John testified that Jesus and his apostles paid taxes both to Caesar and to the temple.
ch48.b027: “⟦Q 185:3.2⟧And now about the third accusation against you, are you the king of the Jews?⟦/Q⟧” There was a tone of possibly sincere inquiry in Pilate’s voice, and Jesus smiled at him. “⟦Q 185:3.2⟧Pilate, do you ask this for yourself, or do you take this question from these others, my accusers?⟦/Q⟧” With partial indignation Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew?” Then Jesus said: “⟦Q 185:3.3⟧Do you not perceive that my kingdom is not of this world? If my kingdom were of this world, surely would my disciples fight that I should not be delivered into the hands of the Jews.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 185:3.4⟧Then you are a king after all?⟦/Q⟧” said Pilate. Jesus answered: “⟦Q 185:3.4⟧Yes, I am such a king, and my kingdom is the family of the faith sons of my Father who is in heaven. For this purpose was I born into this world, even that I should show my Father to all men and bear witness to the truth of God. And even now do I declare to you that every one who loves the truth hears my voice.⟦/Q⟧”
ch48.b028: Then said Pilate, half in ridicule and half in sincerity, “Truth, what is truth—who knows?”
ch48.b029: He could not fathom the spiritual kingdom, but one look at this gentle and weary, yet majestic and upright, man convinced him that he was no dangerous revolutionary. He went back out and said, “⟦Q 185:3.7⟧I have examined this man, and I find no fault in him.⟦/Q⟧” The accusers broke into angry shouts, and one Sanhedrist cried that this man stirred up the people, “⟦Q 185:3.7⟧beginning in Galilee and continuing throughout all Judea.⟦/Q⟧” At the word Galilee, Pilate saw a way to escape the decision. He sent Jesus to Herod Antipas, who was in the city for the Passover.
ch48.b030: Herod was staying in the old Maccabean palace. He had long been curious about Jesus and hoped to see him perform some wonder. He never for a moment recalled the lad who had once stood before him in Sepphoris, pleading for a just decision about the money due his father, killed in an accident on a public building. For some fifteen minutes Herod questioned and taunted him and dared him to work a miracle, but Jesus would not answer. Then, after making fun of him for a time, Herod dressed him in an old purple royal robe and sent him back to Pilate. He had long feared that Jesus might be John the Baptist risen from the dead; now, seeing that this was a very different sort of man, he was relieved of that fear.
ch48.b032: Pilate went out to the judgment seat on the front steps and told the chief priests that neither he nor Herod had found anything worthy of death in this man; he would chastise him and release him. Just then a vast crowd came up to ask, according to custom, for the release of a prisoner at the Passover. Pilate thought he had found his way out, for Jesus had so recently been a favorite of the multitudes. But the name the crowd was calling was Barabbas, a noted political agitator and murderous robber lately taken in the act of robbery and murder on the Jericho road.
ch48.b033: “⟦Q 185:5.4⟧Which, therefore, would you prefer that I release to you, this Barabbas, the murderer, or this Jesus of Galilee?⟦/Q⟧” The chief priests and councilors shouted at the top of their voices, “Barabbas, Barabbas!” and the people quickly joined them. Jesus could be a hero when he drove the money-changers from the temple, but not as a nonresisting prisoner on trial for his life. Pilate, angered, asked how they could prefer a murderer to a man “⟦Q 185:5.6⟧whose worst crime is that he figuratively calls himself the king of the Jews.⟦/Q⟧” It was not a wise thing to say. To call this meek prisoner “the king of the Jews” insulted everything the proud nation held sacred, and they shouted all the louder for Barabbas.
ch48.b034: While Pilate hesitated, a messenger brought him a sealed note from his wife, Claudia. “⟦Q 185:5.8⟧I pray you have nothing to do with this innocent and just man whom they call Jesus. I have suffered many things in a dream this night because of him.⟦/Q⟧” While he read it, the rulers went freely through the crowd, urging them to call for Barabbas and for Jesus’ crucifixion. At last Pilate asked, “⟦Q 185:5.9⟧What shall I do with him who is called the king of the Jews?⟦/Q⟧” And they all shouted with one accord, “Crucify him! Crucify him!” “⟦Q 185:5.10⟧Why would you crucify this man? What evil has he done?⟦/Q⟧” But they only cried out the more, “Crucify him! Crucify him!”
ch48.b036: Pilate would make one last appeal to their pity. He ordered Jesus scourged, though Roman law allowed scourging only for those already condemned to die by crucifixion. In the open courtyard of the praetorium the soldiers put the purple robe on him again, plaited a crown of thorns and set it on his brow, and put a reed in his hand as a mock scepter. They knelt before him and mocked him, saying, “Hail, king of the Jews!” They spat on him and struck him in the face, and one of them took the reed from his hand and struck him on the head. Before the scourgers had finished, Pilate ordered them to stop.
ch48.b037: Then he led out the bleeding and lacerated prisoner and presented him to the multitude. “⟦Q 185:6.3⟧Behold the man! Again I declare to you that I find no crime in him, and having scourged him, I would release him.⟦/Q⟧” There stood Jesus of Nazareth in an old purple robe, a crown of thorns piercing his kindly brow, his face bloodstained, his form bowed down with suffering and grief. The sight sent a mighty shudder through the realms of a vast universe, but it did not touch the hearts of those who had resolved to destroy him. When they recovered from the first shock, they only shouted the louder, “⟦Q 185:6.5⟧Crucify him! Crucify him! Crucify him!⟦/Q⟧”
ch48.b038: Then the high priest stepped up to Pilate and declared: “⟦Q 185:6.7⟧We have a sacred law, and by that law this man ought to die because he made himself out to be the Son of God.⟦/Q⟧” At this Pilate was all the more afraid. He remembered his wife’s note and the Greek tales of gods coming down to earth, and he trembled at the thought that Jesus might be a divine being. He led Jesus inside again, sat down beside him, and asked, “⟦Q 185:7.1⟧Where do you come from? Really, who are you?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus looked him straight in the face but did not answer. “⟦Q 185:7.2⟧Do you refuse to speak to me? Do you not realize that I still have power to release you or to crucify you?⟦/Q⟧” Then Jesus said: “⟦Q 185:7.2⟧You could have no power over me except it were permitted from above. … But you are not so guilty since you are ignorant of the gospel. He who betrayed me and he who delivered me to you, they have the greater sin.⟦/Q⟧”
ch48.b040: Pilate was just about ready to release Jesus when Caiaphas came up, shook an avenging finger in his face, and said so that the whole multitude could hear: “⟦Q 185:7.5⟧If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend, and I will see that the emperor knows all.⟦/Q⟧” That public threat was too much. Fear for his own fortunes now eclipsed everything else. Pilate had Jesus brought out before the judgment seat, pointed to him, and said tauntingly, “Behold your king.” The Jews answered, “Away with him. Crucify him!” “Shall I crucify your king?” “⟦Q 185:7.5⟧Yes, crucify him! We have no king but Caesar.⟦/Q⟧”
ch48.b041: Here stood the Son of God incarnate as the Son of Man. He had been arrested without indictment, accused without evidence, adjudged without witnesses, punished without a verdict, and now he was to be condemned to die by a judge who confessed he could find no fault in him. Pilate had recently been reprimanded by Caesar, and he dared not risk a riot at Passover time. He ordered the release of Barabbas, and the mob cheered.
ch48.b042: Then he called for a basin and some water, and there before the multitude he washed his hands, saying: “⟦Q 185:8.2⟧I am innocent of the blood of this man. You are determined that he shall die, but I have found no guilt in him. See you to it. The soldiers will lead him forth.⟦/Q⟧” And the mob cheered and replied, “⟦Q 185:8.2⟧His blood be on us and on our children.⟦/Q⟧”
